newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain bourse bulls lured by share split vogue.
newsitem.headline: Spain bourse bulls lured by share split vogue.

text.p: Share splits are all the rage in Spain, with the trend seen providing yet more fuel for a stock market already burgeoning with retail investor funds, analysts said on Tuesday.
Bankinter was the latest to jump on the bandwagon, earlier announcing a three-for-one split. This came hot on the heels of Gas Natural on Monday, and Banco Bilbao Vizcaya on Friday.
Before this most recent spate, Banco Popular had announced a split in April, following habitual trend-setter Banco Santander.

"It's really a bit of a mirage. Splits are fashionable at the moment as part of the current stock market fever. But it does have a pychological effect for the small shareholder, and they're the ones who are buying stocks at the moment," said a trader at a Spanish bank.
The bourse continues to hit a raft of highs, and analysts are loathe to make fresh indices forecasts having already seen year-end targets pulverised by the end of the first quarter.
Stocks have been boosted by domestic money seeking higher yields after traditional savings instruments have lost some of their allure amid declining key money rates.

"One fundamental reason which explains the good phase in the Spanish bourse is the need to find investments with relatively attractive returns vis a vis expectations of further interest rate cuts," said Felix Gonzalez, head of research at Beta Capital brokerage.

Splits make shares more accessible to the man on the street, increasingly liquidity by raising the number of shares quoted, although they do not change the fundamental valuation of a listed firm, analysts said.

"Small shareholders do look at prices in pesetas. The average person doesn't think in terms of price earnings ratios, but rather that something which costs 1,000 pesetas is automatically cheaper than something which costs 30,000 pesetas," said Cayetano Cornet, analyst at Credit Lyonnais Securities Espana.
And as regards future split candidates, analysts were not ruling out any stock trading above 10,000 pesetas per share.
"It seems a bit daft, but you could safely say that the way things are going, practically any stock with a share price of over five figures could be a candidate," said an analyst at a foreign bank.
One potential candidate was considered to be electricity firm Endesa, currently trading at around 11,900 pesetas --near its all-time high-- and due to be further privatised in the autumn.

"(A share split) wouldn't be a bad thing for Endesa at all. Anything which increases the attractiveness for the small shareholder ahead of a public offering is of interest. But whether it's likely or not, I couldn't say," said Credit Lyonnais' Cornet.
